rows.subtype: Loud reactions online and voice notes [Mismatch]
rows.description: A young professional reads ALL CAPS, many exclamation marks or a shouted voice note as excitement or anger, and cannot be sure which. Checking tone with a quick call or question avoids a needless quarrel.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A young adult hears a scream in a street or hostel and weighs whether it is play, a film or danger. Calling emergency services or a security guard is wiser than either ignoring it or rushing in alone.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A young adult hears a groan or moan and must judge whether it is jest, tiredness or real pain. When a person seems unwell, asking and offering help or calling for medical aid is wiser than assuming exaggeration.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.description: A young professional hears a throat clear or a grunt and wonders if it means disagreement, a need to speak or just a tickle. Cues like this are weak; asking a follow-up such as did you want to add something is fair.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Oops, ouch and apologetic sounds at work [Expressing]
rows.description: A young professional says oops after an error or ouch to a hard remark to show mild dismay. Such small sounds can lighten a moment but should not replace a proper apology or fix when the mistake mattered.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Um, uh and filler in public speaking [Regulating]
rows.description: A young professional replaces um and uh with a pause while presenting, which reads as more confident. Fillers are normal and do not mean ignorance, and a short silence can help both speaker and audience.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Cultural norms about volume and pitch [Mismatch]
rows.description: A young professional working across cultures finds that loud talk may signal friendliness in one place and aggression in another, and soft speech may mean respect or shyness. Avoid judging character from volume alone.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: admiration, hostility, shyness

rows.description: A young adult facing an angry customer or colleague speaks slower, lower and softer to calm the room. A steady tone signals control and care, while matching the anger tends to escalate; leaving is right if threats appear.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Harsh voice at work and de-escalation [Interpreting]
rows.description: A young professional facing a harsh, raspy or strained voice from an angry client should treat it as a sign of high arousal. Lowering own volume, slowing down and acknowledging the concern usually calms the exchange.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Voice on calls and voice notes [Mismatch]
rows.description: Breathy, nasal or flat voices on phone lines, voice notes and video calls lose visual cues and add compression noise. A tired-sounding voice may just be a poor connection, so checking in beats guessing.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22
related mind states: tiredness, relief from stress
